fields.Q1:
WHAT IS STANDING AROUND THIS ROOM MADE OF?**
At the size shown, I cannot tell. It is a near-black band with a faint blue-grey cast. If you magnify it, it is cut grey stone — a large plain slab course over a course of smaller blocks — but nothing about that survives at 1:1.
fields.Q1_WHY: The standing band (y199–262 top, y776–831 bottom, x0–56 left, x697–749 right) averages RGB (10.9, 9.7, 10.5). Its 95th percentile is 26 and its absolute maximum across the entire structure is 47. Zero percent of standing-surface pixels exceed luminance 128; 0.52% exceed 64; 92% sit below 16. The adjacent ground runs mean 80 with 40% of pixels above 64. The structure is roughly one-eighth the brightness of what it encloses. There is not enough signal in it to name a material — it's a hue, not a surface.
fields.Q2:
SOLID MASS, OR A FLAT PATTERN AROUND THE EDGE?**
Flat pattern — with one instructive exception.

Averaging 200px of width, the vertical profile through the top band is: y197 = 1.4 (void), y199–229 = a flat 9.5–10.8, a 2px dark seam at y231–233 = 3.5, y235–261 = 6–8, another 2px dark seam at y263 = 4.4, then ground climbing 6.7 → 20.9 → 45. So there are two 32px strips stacked to one 64px cell, and the *lower* strip is darker than the upper by ~3 levels. If that lower strip is a near-facing side and the upper is a top face, the entire read of "this thing has height" is carried by a 3/255 step. It isn't legible.

The decisive test is light response. Sampling the top band along its length against the ground 40px below it, at matched distance from the figure: at x=380 (closest approach, ~276px from the torch) the ground reads 45.1 and the wall reads 13.9; at x=20 (473px away) ground reads 6.3 and wall reads 6.0. The ground swings 39 levels across the frame; the wall swings 11. The bottom band is worse — 7.9 to 12.5 across the entire 750px width, essentially constant regardless of distance. **The standing structure is not lit by the light source.** It carries a near-constant ambient term. Mass that doesn't take light isn't mass; it's a border colour.

The exception: one wall cell sits inside the torch cone at x185–249, y455–519. There, magnified, it reads correctly and well — a striated slab on top, four or five smaller blocks below, a hard seam between them, a black crack running down through both. The asset is solid. Nowhere else in the frame is it lit enough to prove it.
fields.Q3:
WHERE EXACTLY DOES THE GROUND STOP?**
Top edge: y=263, a 2-pixel dark seam (row average drops to 4.4 from 8.3 above and 6.7 below). Across it: nothing but a value dip and a change of block scale. No bevel, no highlight lip, no cast shadow, no occlusion. The transition is complete in 2 pixels and is the same 2 pixels everywhere along its length.

The other side of that band is harder: at y=198 the value jumps from 1.4 to 10.2 in two pixels, and that boundary is dead straight from x=0 to x=310 and again x=503 to x=749. That is a visibility cut, not architecture — so the structure is exactly 64px (one cell) deep everywhere, and you cannot see whether it continues.

The one lit stub at (185,455) also just stops — its bottom edge at y=519 has no contact shadow. A block standing up with a light 150px to its east throws nothing west of itself.
fields.Q4:
WHAT IS HOLDING THIS PLACE TOGETHER?**
At 1:1, **NOTHING**. There is not one visible fastening, tie, brace, prop or patch anywhere in the frame.

Under magnification there is one: at x137–155, y198–235, a vertical shaft crossed by three horizontal bars — a driven pin with washers, or a bracket. It is exactly the fitting this fiction wants. Its brightest pixels measure 11 against a surrounding wall of 9. **Two levels out of 255.** There is a second candidate — a vertical bar at x565–575, y192–232, mean 6.0 against wall 8.4 — reading as a driven rod, also invisible. Someone drew the repairs. Nobody can see them.
fields.Q5:
BUILT, OR AN IMAGE REPEATED?**
Built. I cross-correlated all 18 full 64px wall cells in the top and bottom bands, after subtracting each cell's per-row profile so shared course structure wouldn't mask the answer. Of 190 pairs, 188 sit near zero — the per-cell detail is genuinely unique. The crack marks land at scattered offsets within their cells ((x−57) mod 64 = 19, 8, 39, 16, 37, 5, 47, 13, 29, 21, 28, 51, 58, 25, 46, 23), so nothing is stamped at a fixed position.

Two pairs are not unique: bottom band x121 vs x249 correlates at **0.998** (raw luminance difference: mean −0.02, max 2.33, std 0.17 — the same bitmap), and x505 vs x569 at **0.974** — those two are *adjacent*, the same stone twice in a row. Two duplicates out of 190 is a variety library doing its job with one slip.
fields.Q6:
WOULD YOU BELIEVE THIS SHIPPED?** YES.
Merely competent, or genuinely good? **Merely competent.** Not because the asset is weak — the asset is better than competent, and I can prove it from the one cell that happens to fall in the light. The delivered frame is merely competent because everything good about the walls is below threshold. Quality that cannot be perceived at the shipping size does not count as quality.
fields.Q7:
WHAT CAN YOU ACTUALLY SEE ON THE STANDING SURFACES AT 1:1?**
Blank. On my first pass at 1:1 I read the top of the frame as "a corridor going north" and did not register that there was a wall at all — I took the whole visible field as one continuous surface. The standing surfaces carry no legible face at 1:1 anywhere in this image except the single cell at x185–249, y455–519, where the slab/brick split, the seam and the crack are all readable without magnification.

Distance dependence: yes, but the wrong way round. It's not that the wall fades with distance — it's flat at ~10 whether it's 276px from the torch or 500px. It becomes visible only where the ground beside it is dark enough not to drown it, which is the far corners, where there's nothing to see anyway.
fields.Q7_WHY: Checked at 1:1 — x0–310 y199–262; x503–749 y199–262; x311–502 y199–262 (the brightest available wall, mean 16.3, max 36); x0–56 y263–775; x697–749 y263–775; x0–749 y776–831; and x185–249 y455–519 (the only one that read). Had to magnify (3–8× nearest, plus gamma 0.30–0.35) — x110–180 y190–265 to find the crossbar fitting; x530–620 y190–265 to find the vertical rod; x250–580 y140–320 to find the north opening; x600–750 y760–835. Every structural claim above beyond "it's a dark band" came from the magnified pass.
fields.Q8:
IS THERE ANYTHING YOUR EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO?**
Yes, three things.

First: the horizontal seam. It falls at y=231 and y=263 in the top band and at the matching offset in every other band — the same 2px dark line at the same place in every cell, running unbroken from x=0 to x=749. Once seen it's the only rhythm in the structure, and it's a ruler line.

Second: the two-strip split (32px + 32px) with the same proportion and same value relationship in every cell. Cell content varies; cell *scheme* never does.

Third, and worse for the fiction: the damage is metered. Counting near-black crack pixels per cell along the bottom band gives 22, 16, 10, 16, 10, 14, 32, 14, 14, 22 — mean 17, and only one cell out of ten more than 1.7× the mean. Sixteen distinct crack marks in the top band and exactly sixteen in the bottom. The wear is distributed at a constant rate rather than concentrated where something happened to it.
fields.Q9:
WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS?**
Nothing — and I mean that literally, as a fill. The region x0–310 and x505–749 above y=198 is **98.62% a single colour, RGB(1,1,2)**, over 107,000 pixels. The remaining 1.4% is entirely the minimap and the zoom buttons sitting on top of it. No gradient, no noise, no fog, no dither. Its boundary is a hard two-pixel cut at exactly y=198, dead straight, and vertical cuts at x=310 and x=503.

So it isn't more of the same stuff, it isn't another room, and it isn't space. It's a lid. The frame doesn't say "you can't see past this" — it says "there is no past this." For an underworld whose whole premise is that it continues in every direction and has for longer than records go back, a flat monochrome fill with a straight edge is the one thing it must not read as.
fields.Q10:
COULD YOU TELL A WAY THROUGH FROM A DEAD END WITHOUT WALKING INTO IT?**
I found the gap: it is one cell wide, x=377 to x=440, running north from the room's top edge at y=263 up to the top of the frame.

I could not read it from the structure, and I'll be exact about how I got it wrong. On my first 1:1 pass I identified a passage at x311–502 — three cells wide. That is not the passage; that's the shape of the visible region. The real opening is the middle third of it, and I only separated it from its flanking wall cells at 4× magnification.

The numbers say why. Over y205–258: the open ground in the gap averages 19.7, the wall to its left averages 16.8, the wall to its right 14.8. **A three-to-five level difference out of 255** between "floor you can walk down" and "stone you cannot." That is not a passage; that is a notch in a pattern.

What told me a way through existed was the black — the void's rectangular cut-out reaching north. The architecture contributed nothing. Which means the player reads the fog-of-war shape, not the level.
fields.Q11:
HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED TO THIS STRUCTURE?**
It is cracked, evenly, everywhere, at a constant rate, and that is all I can read. Thirty-two crack marks across the two horizontal bands, distributed at ~1.4 per cell in both, with no clustering, no breach, no place where the damage means something. No spall, no missing block, no bulge, no soot, no water line, no repair I can see at size. There is no direction to the wear — nothing indicates which side the pressure came from or which century did it.

Read from: the per-cell crack counts above, the scattered-but-uniform in-cell offsets, and the fact that the two visible fittings (x137–155 and x565–575) sit at 2 levels of contrast. Four hundred years of a company holding a line ought to leave a wall that is *unevenly* mended — a stretch that's all pin and timber next to a stretch nobody's touched. This one has been aged with a filter, not used.
fields.CULL: Walls receive no light — 0% of standing pixels above 128/255; every crack, course and repair is dark-on-dark.
fields.FLIP LIST:
- Put the walls in the same lighting model as the ground: the standing band must brighten with proximity to the carried light, not sit at a constant ~10/255 while the floor beside it swings 6→45.
- Separate the near face from the top face by a real value step. The current 3/255 difference across the y=231 seam cannot carry the read of thickness.
- Raise the passage-vs-wall contrast at x377–440, y199–262. Three levels of luminance is not a legible way through; the player is currently navigating by fog-of-war shape.
- Give the void past y=198 something other than a flat RGB(1,1,2) fill with a straight edge — depth cue, falloff, or a hint of continuing structure. Right now the underworld has a ceiling.
- Break the metering: concentrate damage and visible repair (pin, rope, salvaged timber) in a few cells at contrast that survives at 1:1, and leave others clean, instead of ~1.4 evenly-spread crack marks in every cell. While there, deduplicate the adjacent identical tiles at x505 and x569 in the bottom band.

*Model: Claude Opus 5 (1M context).*
